description: NASA’s SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared bands: over a billion objects. Pluto was found by comparing 2 photos. We’re a Manila team led by Clarence (UP Manila CS, GCash ML intern, placed in 3 of 3 hackathons) building a tool that lines up SPHEREx images, flags what moved, and shows each object’s infrared spectrum. Pluto’s finder had two photos. We have a script.
summary: Wanderer is a web tool that measures moving objects in NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey. IRSA's Moving Object Search Tool lists which SPHEREx images caught an asteroid or comet but measures nothing, and IRSA's Spectrophotometry Tool only measures fixed positions. We follow the object along its JPL track, measure it in every frame, and return its 0.75 to 5 micron spectrum as a CSV or VOTable, one row per frame. It ships with the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS (116 frames, with water, CO2 and CO bands standing out) and 10 asteroids. A second tool, Vet a Field, sorts every change between visits in a patch of sky into known asteroid, bright-star leftover, cosmic ray, detector edge, cannot confirm or unexplained, and shows the evidence for each. It also covers the challenge's must-have: type an RA and Dec and the SPHEREx images of that spot play like a flipbook, with Gaia positions marked. We claim no discovery. The depth we reach is about magnitude 18 to 19, far too shallow for Planet X, so the value is in faster, checkable measurements of objects we already know.
details:
What it does

NASA's archive shows which SPHEREx images caught a comet or asteroid, but not how bright it was in them. Wanderer measures it. For the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, IRSA publishes the frames and predicted positions but no extracted spectrum; Wanderer returns 116 measured frames from 0.75 to 4.95 microns as a download. It has three parts.

  1. Moving-object spectra. IRSA's Moving Object Search Tool (MOST) tells you which SPHEREx images caught an asteroid or comet, but it measures nothing. IRSA's Spectrophotometry Tool measures a fixed position, so it cannot follow a mover. We fill that gap. For each object we ask JPL Horizons where it was, as seen from the SPHEREx spacecraft, at the middle of every exposure. We cut that spot out of the calibrated image, find the object, sum its light in a stated aperture, subtract the sky, and read the wavelength from the image's own per-pixel wavelength map. The result is a table with one row per frame: time, predicted and measured position, wavelength, flux, error, signal to noise and quality flags. It downloads as CSV, VOTable or JSON.

    It ships with the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS (116 frames from 0.75 to 4.95 microns; water at 2.7 microns, carbon dioxide at 4.26 microns and carbon monoxide at 4.67 microns stand out, in line with the SPHEREx team's published result) and 10 asteroids, including C, S and M types (21 Lutetia, 22 Kalliope, 24 Themis, 52 Europa, 243 Ida, 951 Gaspra and others), each with 98 to 185 measured frames and a median position offset under 2.3 arcseconds.
  2. Vet a Field. Anyone hunting for new objects in SPHEREx, such as Backyard Worlds volunteers, needs to know whether a dot that changed between visits is real. For a patch of sky we find every change and sort it into known asteroid (checked against JPL), bright-star leftover (checked against Gaia DR3), cosmic ray, detector edge or mask, cannot confirm, or unexplained, and we show the evidence for each verdict. In a 145-change field near the ecliptic it found the 2 known asteroids within 7 arcseconds of JPL, and left 5 changes unexplained for a person to check rather than calling them new. We also found that SPHEREx's own TRANSIENT flag marks only 7 of the 21 cosmic rays we identified, a concrete note for the mission's data team.
  3. The RA/Dec flipbook and sky map. Type a position or a name and the SPHEREx images of that spot play like a short video, one frame per visit, with Gaia positions and difference images. As a check of our code, it measures Barnard's Star moving 10.55 plus or minus 0.71 arcseconds per year against Gaia's 10.36.

Benefits and impact

Going from MOST's image list to a measured spectrum otherwise takes hours of custom scripting per object. We make it a download. Every number comes from a script in our repository that can be rerun, and every page states its limits.

Honest limits

Do the 5 unexplained changes hint at Planet X? No. We reach about magnitude 18 to 19, far too shallow, and we make no discovery claim. Spectra are flux, not reflectance: the Sun's spectrum and thermal emission are not removed, and rotation mixes with wavelength between frames. Comet flux depends on the aperture, which we state.

Tools

Python 3.12 with uv, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Requests, Pillow, reproject and pytest for the pipeline. TypeScript, React 19, Vite and Aladin Lite for the web app. Data from the NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx archive, JPL Horizons and the JPL small-body identification service, and ESA Gaia DR3. Hosting on Vercel.

What we considered

We first built a viewer, then asked whether a SPHEREx scientist would use it. Most of what a viewer does, IRSA already does. So we moved the project to the one thing IRSA's tools do not do: measure objects that move.
